First listed 2026-07-15 · episode or wrap

Beyond Ozempic: The Next Wave of Biotech Winners with Boris Peaker

Peaker explains trial costs, early-stage selection risk, China sourcing and why oncology and orphan diseases attract development capital. He highlights pancreatic-cancer RAS inhibition, immune resets, gene editing and muscle-preserving obesity therapies, while questioning rapid AI-driven productivity gains. Eisman adopts several explanations in his recap. Daraxonrasib efficacy and subsequent approval are verified, but the recap misstates the control treatment. FDA rules do not categorically require all pivotal patients to be American. GLP-1 lean-mass data need careful interpretation, and Lilly commercial strength does not establish permanent victory over Novo.

Substack · 2026-07-15 ↗
Useful development-economics framework with several factual overstatements. Clinical benefit, commercial attractiveness and stock returns are kept separate. Most company-specific long-run commercial outcomes remain unresolved or genuinely future-dated.

Source version, speaker attribution and transcript cautions

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

publisher machine transcript with speaker markers

SPEAKER_01 is Steve Eisman and SPEAKER_00 is Boris Peaker, established by named introduction and dialogue. Several SPEAKER_00 blocks contain short Eisman prompts; standalone assertions are assigned from conversational context.

  • Introductory audio/captions skip from about 77 to 96 seconds and several later phrases are incomplete.
  • Peaker, daraxonrasib, retatrutide, Novo Nordisk and PCSK9 are misspelled in machine captions.
  • The $1.3 billion acquisition-capacity statement is explicitly corrected to $1.3 trillion.
  • Phase/stage terminology is colloquial; cancer stage must not be confused with trial phase.
  • The pancreatic trial involved previously treated metastatic disease and chemotherapy controls, not all newly diagnosed patients or an untreated control.
  • Lean mass and skeletal muscle are not interchangeable measurements.
  • HeLa historical details are incidental and omitted from material claims; they should not be relied on as a scientific chronology.

How he reasons here

  • Evaluate trial economics by disease, endpoint and time to informative data.
  • Early selective samples may not predict broad population outcomes.
  • Separate statistically significant benefit from cure and normal life expectancy.
  • Distinguish clinical development, regulatory approval and commercial value.
  • Test AI productivity through failure rates and full development cycles.
  • Consider patent expirations and acquisition proceeds as capital-recycling drivers.

Tools and charts discussed

Mentioned in the transcript; visual charts have not all been inspected.

  • Per-patient clinical-trial budgets
  • Phase transition success rates
  • Median survival and control-arm comparisons
  • Tumor sequencing and mutation burden
  • DXA body composition versus functional outcomes
  • Actuarial life-expectancy comparison
  • Annual novel FDA approvals
  • Biotech IPO, secondary and venture financing
  • Patent-expiry revenue and acquisition capacity
